subtype: Approach: gliding without pedals first to find balance [Thinking]
passage: I'm Samir, and I live in the flat next to Baljeet's. On Sunday I saw her lower her cycle seat until her feet touched the ground, and then walk the cycle along the path, pushing off with her feet. "What are you doing?" I asked. "No pedals yet," she said. "Balance is the hard bit. Pedalling can wait." She kept pushing, and each time she lifted both feet for a moment longer. After ten minutes she glided almost to the gate with her legs stretched out. "See? I'm not falling," she said, grinning. I had never thought to try it like that.

qa.q: What did Baljeet do to the seat of the cycle?
qa.a: Baljeet lowered the seat until her feet touched the ground.

qa.q: How did Baljeet feel about her plan to learn balance before pedalling?
qa.a: Baljeet felt patient and confident: she thought balance was the hard part and pedalling could wait, and she grinned as she said, "See? I'm not falling."

qa.q: What alternative approach could Baljeet try, and why?
qa.a: Baljeet could ask a friend to hold the seat while she pedals, or practise a slow slope. Both help her learn balance with some support.

qa.q: How does Samir see Baljeet's method?
qa.a: Samir had never thought to try it like that and watches with curiosity, so Samir sees a clever idea and probably wants to learn it.

grounding: A girl lowers the seat and glides with both feet up first, reasoning that balance is the hard part and pedalling can wait until she has it.

subtype: Approach: gliding without pedals first to find balance [Thinking]
passage:
Sunday: Rehana's toes only reached the ground on tiptoe, and every time she tried to pedal she tipped over. Her brother Rafiq offered to push her. She shook her head.
Tuesday: "The pedals aren't the problem," she told Rafiq, pulling the seat down to the lowest notch. "Staying up is. If I can't stay up, pedalling just makes me fall faster." She walked the cycle along, then pushed with both feet and lifted them, gliding for two seconds. Then three.
Friday: She glided across the whole courtyard with her feet up, counting aloud to seven. "Now," she said, "now I'll try the pedals." The first push went round, then the second.

qa.q: How far down did Rehana pull the seat?
qa.a: She pulled it down to the lowest notch.

qa.q: Why did Rehana shake her head when Rafiq offered to push?
qa.a: She wanted to work it out herself; she seems determined and a little stubborn about finding her own way.

qa.q: What else could Rehana try if gliding stops getting better, and why?
qa.a: She could glide down a very gentle slope, because the extra speed makes balance easier to find.

qa.q: How does Rehana's plan look to Rafiq?
qa.a: Rafiq might be puzzled at first that she refuses a push, and then impressed when her gliding works.

grounding: It shows a girl who lowers her seat, glides with her feet up and reasons that balance must come before pedalling.

subtype: Approach: gliding without pedals first to find balance [Thinking]
passage: Pradeep, stop kicking that cycle and come sit with your Nani. You think Ira Nani was born riding? In our village there was one cycle, my father's, big and black, and my feet could not touch the ground from the seat. Every time I tried the pedals I fell, and my brother laughed. So one afternoon I sat under the neem and asked myself which part was hard. Not the pedals. Any fool can push pedals. The hard part was staying up. I borrowed the tailor's daughter's small cycle, let the seat right down so my feet were flat, and pushed along the dirt road, lifting my feet, gliding. A little further each day. Only when I could glide past the well did I try the pedals. It took one go.

qa.a: Ira borrowed the tailor's daughter's small cycle.

qa.q: How did young Ira probably feel when her brother laughed at her falls?
qa.a: Young Ira probably felt hurt and embarrassed, and it made Ira more determined to work it out.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Ira's story, and what else could she have tried?
qa.a: The turning point was Ira asking which part was hard and choosing to practise balance first; Ira could also have asked someone to hold the seat on the big cycle.

qa.q: How might Ira's brother have seen her gliding along the dirt road?
qa.a: Ira's brother may have thought it looked silly at first, then been surprised when Ira rode the first time she tried the pedals.

grounding: An elder tells how, as a girl, she lowered a seat and glided with her feet up, reasoning that balance came before pedalling.
